title: Network foundation (hub-and-spoke topology)
hook: Hub-and-spoke networking centralizes shared connectivity in a hub Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) while workload accounts attach as spokes via AWS Transit Gateway (TGW) or VPC peering. IP Address Management (IPAM) prevents CIDR collisions.

blocks.text: Hub VPC hosts shared services: egress NAT, firewall appliances (GWLB), DNS resolver endpoints, and TGW attachments. Spoke VPCs in workload accounts connect to hub for hybrid connectivity (Direct Connect, VPN) and inter-spoke routing. AWS Network Firewall or third-party NGFW often sits in inspection VPC. IPAM pools allocate non-overlapping CIDR blocks per account.

entries.plainDefinition: Regional hub connecting VPCs and VPN/DX

blocks.text: Interviewers draw hub-spoke on whiteboards for enterprise AWS. Wrong CIDR planning blocks peering. Centralized egress simplifies allow-listing but creates chokepoint — know the tradeoff.

blocks.title: Interview framing
blocks.body: Say: hub VPC + TGW, spokes per account/env, IPAM for CIDR, centralized egress with inspection option.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Plan IPAM pools
items.body: Top-level pool; allocate /16 or /20 per account from pool.

items.title: Deploy hub VPC
items.body: TGW, NAT, optional Network Firewall, Route53 resolver rules.

items.title: Attach spokes
items.body: Workload VPC TGW attachment; propagate routes via TGW route tables.

items.title: Segment routing
items.body: Separate TGW route tables for prod vs dev isolation.

diagram.title: Hub and spoke
diagram.source:
flowchart TB
  DX[Direct Connect] --> HUB[Hub VPC / TGW]
  HUB --> S1[Spoke dev VPC]
  HUB --> S2[Spoke prod VPC]
  HUB --> FW[Inspection VPC]

snippet.label: Create IPAM pool
snippet.code:
aws ec2 create-ipam-pool \
  --ipam-id ipam-abc \
  --address-family ipv4 \
  --locale us-east-1 \
  --allocation-min-netmask-length 16
snippet.explanation: Central pool prevents overlapping spoke CIDRs.

snippet.label: TGW attachment
snippet.code:
aws ec2 create-transit-gateway-vpc-attachment \
  --transit-gateway-id tgw-abc \
  --vpc-id vpc-spoke \
  --subnet-ids subnet-a subnet-b
snippet.explanation: Connect spoke VPC to hub transit.

snippet.label: TGW route table association
snippet.code:
SpokeRoute:
  Type: AWS::EC2::TransitGatewayRoute
  Properties:
    TransitGatewayRouteTableId: !Ref ProdRouteTable
    DestinationCidrBlock: 10.20.0.0/16
    TransitGatewayAttachmentId: !Ref SpokeAttachment
snippet.explanation: Route propagation controls which spokes talk to which.

snippet.label: Reachability Analyzer
snippet.code:
aws ec2 create-network-insights-path \
  --source vpc-spoke \
  --destination vpc-hub \
  --protocol TCP \
  --destination-port 443

blocks.title: Cloud vs app patterns
rows: Flat VPC peering mesh — scales poorly

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Overlapping CIDRs block peering/TGW routes. Full mesh VPC peering at 20+ VPCs. Single TGW route table for prod and dev.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: IPAM utilization dashboard; TGW route table segmentation audit; Reachability Analyzer paths documented per connection.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: VPC peering mesh for 30 accounts — rejected. Strong answer: TGW hub-spoke, IPAM, segmented route tables.

interviewTakeaways: Hub-spoke: central TGW hub, spokes per account/VPC, IPAM for CIDR.
Overlapping CIDRs are fatal — plan with IPAM upfront.
Segment TGW route tables for prod/dev isolation.
60s: Hub VPC with TGW, spokes attach, IPAM allocates CIDRs, optional inspection VPC. Avoid peering mesh at scale.
Follow-up: centralized vs distributed NAT tradeoff?
commonPitfalls: CIDR overlap discovered after account vending — expensive fix.
Strong answer: IPAM first, then hub-spoke TGW, segmented routes.
VPC peering full mesh at enterprise scale.
Prod and dev on same TGW route table.

jsTsCorrelations.note: Hub VPC like API gateway for network — central entry for hybrid and shared services.
Spoke accounts like TS project references — explicit interfaces (TGW routes) between them.
